title: Shifting the focus
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino, a secondary science teacher, reflects on a bottom-set class where six loud students absorbed her attention while quiet, compliant students like Helen went unnoticed. Her central move is to shift the teacher's focus from the disruptive minority to the fourteen students who follow instructions, and to let routines do the work of changing class norms. She describes limited, consistent routines, explicit behaviour expectations with praise for kindness, a fixed weekly homework format that feeds the next lesson's Do Now, and silent in-class practice of key diagrams and concepts. The payoff is that Helen, who thought she had a bad memory, begins to answer confidently because compliance is rewarded with success. The piece is a modest, concrete case that classroom culture is shifted by what the teacher chooses to reward and attend to.
points: Where a teacher's attention goes shapes class culture, so redirecting it from the few loud students to the many quiet, compliant ones is itself a behaviour strategy.
A small set of fixed routines for entry, Do Now, mini-whiteboards and independent practice, added gradually, gives anxious students predictability.
Reusing homework questions in the next lesson's Do Now turns doing homework into visible confidence and participation.
Explicit expectations paired with public praise for supportive behaviour can pull in students who do not usually show it.
Time for silent practice recalling diagrams and sequences models the revision habits the teacher wants students to use at home.
quotes: I started this year by shifting the focus to students like Helen. Because when I actually thought about it, in a class of 20 students, 6 of them made all the noise.

Every lesson begins in exactly the same way: students enter quietly, sit down, and start working on the Do Now questions that are displayed on the board. If a student doesn’t know an answer, they are meant to start the sentence of the answer so that when we discuss these as a class, they can complete the answer with their green pen.

For instance, when students who rehearse a sequence or definition out loud are successful, most of the other students are genuinely happy for their classmate. I’ve noticed that when I comment on how proud I am of the class being supportive of their classmate, the students who don’t usually display this behaviour, join in with celebrating their classmate’s success.

Some of the questions that I set for homework end up in the Do Now in the following lesson. After a while, students who do their homework feel more confident at the start of lessons and are more likely to participate in discussions.
I give students time in lessons to silently practice writing out or drawing important concepts. This is separate to independent practice where students answer questions.

All of this may seem obvious to some but it can be very easy to fall into the habit of focusing on the negative behaviours in the classroom. I have done it too many times before and I simply cannot do this anymore.
